extracted.intended_audience: writers, students and general readers interested in theories of humor and comic writing
extracted.subtask_description: A literary-theoretical account of the psychological sources, forms, and mechanisms of humor, intended to guide understanding and creation of comic effects (e.g., irony, exaggeration, practical jokes, truth-revealing shock).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual impulse as a source of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: A great deal of our pleasure in casual humor is flavored with an emotion from the sphere of sex — our conscious attention plays with the negative while our unconscious takes its fill of a positive satisfaction we do not attend to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: maidenly minds laugh at breaks in meaning that have sexual implication; Freud's account that hilarity is fundamentally sexual explains many laughs but may overgeneralize. Consider unconscious sexual satisfaction as one possible motive behind laughter, particularly for jokes with implied sexual content; be cautious about reducing all humor to sex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish glee (cruelty) from genuine humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter arising from triumphant lust or battle cruelty — a loon-like hysterical giggle at cruel gibes and obscene quips — is not humor but glee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a laugh springs from hostile, cruel pleasure (glee) versus an artful comic insight. If the reaction is whooping at cruelty or obscene mimicry, classify it as glee rather than the art of joking; this affects moral and aesthetic judgment of the comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor that reveals truth (playful exposure of reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: To shock us with the playful precipitation of the 'mist' of pretense and warm us with a clear serious glimpse of the naked movement of life is a universal and joyful way of joking; we are always hungry for the simple truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective humor often provides a concise, serious glimpse of a reality concealed by decorum or self-consciousness. Good jokes can be 'bombs of honesty' dropped into the procession of false fronts; evaluate humor by how well it reveals an interior truth in a playful, not merely insulting, way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor used as a rhetorical dodge (masking truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is often the last weapon of those menaced by a truth — jokers get behind a joke and disappear, meeting a serious thrust with a frivolous rebuff that allows attention to slide off the threatened truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing or using humor rhetorically, distinguish genuine comic exposure from evasive joking that conceals unwillingness to confront a truth. Practical advice: enjoy the joke but return to serious speech to prevent the joker from escaping the thrust of argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shock that exposes a sane reading of an absurd situation
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor can 'bring home' to people by means of a shock the sanity of a situation they thought was insane; making them conscious of life by showing 'you think this is it... well, it isn't, but this is.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a revealing, clarifying shock — a comic action or image that reframes a situation and makes its true character evident. Evaluate such humor by the precision of the reframing and its capacity to elicit recognition rather than mere surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience readiness and tolerance for revealing humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Some people lack deeper wishes or have them so stifled that they resent humor that reveals; they call it 'levity' and wish to segregate it or stigmatize it as not serious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or judging humor, consider audience sensibilities: revealing, truth-exposing humor may offend those who prefer decorum. Effective practitioners modulate exposure to avoid alienating those not prepared for such revelations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor of quantity (exaggeration and understatement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manipulation of mere quantity or degree — magnify a subject plausibly then extremely enough to make belief impossible (exaggeration) or speak with words so slight as to be inadequate (understatement/irony) — produces humor when it reaches impracticability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quantitative variation to the point of impracticability: laugh at the 'too much' or 'too little' rather than the merely large or small. Examples: Rabelais, Mark Twain. Evaluate by the imaginal plausibility and the point at which belief collapses into comic recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irony as saying less to mean more (and related quantitative ironies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Irony originally denotes the humor of understatement (saying little to mean much); it also includes saying too much to mean little, or stating the exact opposite of what is meant — all quantitative shifts with a point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply 'irony' primarily to understatement that functions to mean more; extend to overstatement/opposite statements where appropriate. Good irony balances naturalness and pointedness so the audience perceives the gap between literal and intended meaning (Socrates, Veblen examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility and relation to context create the comic point
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic utterance becomes immortal when it is (1) natural and familiar in form tempting our confidence, (2) concisely inadequate relative to the particular situation, and (3) made adequate by some contextual fact (e.g., the speaker being alive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft jokes that are believable in form but inadequate to the situation, and ensure context supplies the additional layer needed to create the point. Evaluate comedic lines for these three conditions of plausibility, inadequacy, and contextual adequacy (example: 'The reports of my death are grossly exaggerated').

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlap and ambiguity between irony and exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.description: Irony and exaggeration often cannot be clearly distinguished because both manipulate quantitative relations; an understatement can be seen as exaggerated ignorance, and an exaggeration as a form of understatement in intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit the fluid boundary between these devices for subtle effect. When analyzing humor, be aware that what appears as irony may function as exaggeration (and vice versa); the prevailing interpretation depends on perception of quantity (intensive vs. extensive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Irony can be gentle or hostile and serves praise as well as blame
rubrics_metrics.description: Irony has lost some fine sense of measure and in common usage often denotes satiric hostility, but it is also suited to gentle, pure irony (e.g., titles like 'On the Inconveniences Resulting from Being Hanged') and can express praise by emphatic contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using irony, decide whether the aim is ridicule, gentle comic reversal, or laudatory emphasis via contradicted literalness. Evaluate tone carefully: irony's effectiveness depends on audience perception of intent (derisive vs affectionate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical humor: humor of disappointment vs. disturbance
rubrics_metrics.description: Two practical forms: (a) humor of disappointment (Kant) — laughter from a strained expectation suddenly brought to nothing; (b) humor of disturbance (Aristotle) — laughter arising from the 'harmlessly ugly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design practical jokes or scenes that either thwart an expected outcome cleverly or present a disturbingly odd but harmless image. Assess whether the comic emotion comes from frustrated expectation or from encountering a manageable ugly/disturbing object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical humor arises from failures of practical ends (absurdity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical humor often results when purposeful actions are reduced to absurdity — a 'reduction to absurdity' of the whole attitude of our wills (e.g., family in Sunday clothes unable to move the horse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct comic situations by escalating the mismatch between human purpose and outcome until the purpose collapses into absurdity. Evaluate the scenario by how comprehensively it undermines the practical intention and invites sympathetic laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared predicament and sympathetic reverberation increase humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is most hilarious when all present are involved in the same predicament; humor is increased through sympathetic reverberation without possibility of derision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For communal comedic effect, stage situations where audience members recognize themselves jointly implicated; assess whether the setup invites shared, non-derisive amusement rather than humiliation of specific individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance and suffering: avoid humor from immediate real anguish
rubrics_metrics.description: We are not usually able to perceive real anguish as humorous unless the persons involved are far away, long dead, or imaginary; sympathy sets a bound on what we can take playfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect ethical limits: material involving present, real suffering is unlikely to be acceptable comedic material for most audiences. Evaluate jokes for required psychological or temporal distance before deeming them humorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irish bulls / bulls as plausible intellectual nothingness
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'Irish bull' is any remark that seems rotund and meaningful until apprehension arrives and there is simply nothing there — plausibility distinguishes it from pure nonsense and can be developed into a delicate comic charm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tightly plausible but empty statements to elicit delight; judge such lines by their crafted plausibility and the skill of delivery that lands a 'nothing' with playful dexterity (e.g., Lewis Carroll style). Avoid mere nonsense without the plausibility that makes a bull enjoyable.
